questionText: Healthcare is said to create a positive externality of consumption. What does this mean?
answers: When a person consumes healthcare, third parties who did not pay for it also benefit.
When a firm produces healthcare, it creates pollution that harms third parties.
Healthcare is so expensive that only wealthy consumers can afford it.
The demand for healthcare is high because everyone values their own health.

questionText: Vaccinations and regular GP consultations are said to generate positive externalities of consumption. Which statement best explains why?
answers: They are provided free of charge, so consumers pay nothing for them.
They are a necessity, so demand for them is highly inelastic.
They reduce the spread of infectious disease, so people who never attended a consultation also benefit.
Doctors earn high incomes, so the government collects more tax revenue.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: Three curves are labelled on the diagram. What do the abbreviations MPB, MSB and MSC stand for?
answers: Maximum private benefit, maximum social benefit and maximum social cost.
Marginal private benefit, marginal social benefit and marginal social cost.
Market price benefit, market supply benefit and market supply cost.
Mean private benefit, mean social benefit and mean social cost.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: Which curve measures the full benefit society receives from each GP consultation?
answers: MPB, because it shows the benefit to the patient who pays for the consultation.
MSC, because it shows what society gives up to provide each consultation.
Neither curve, because external benefits cannot be shown on a diagram.
MSB, because it includes both the private benefit to the patient and the external benefit to others.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: At every quantity, MSB lies $20 above MPB. What does this vertical gap of $20 measure?
answers: The marginal external benefit — the benefit each consultation gives to people other than the patient.
The marginal private benefit received by the patient.
The marginal cost of supplying one more consultation.
The consumer surplus earned on each consultation.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: Consumers decide how many consultations to buy by weighing up their own private benefit. What quantity does the free market deliver?
answers: 6 million, where MSB intersects MSC.
4 million, where MPB intersects MSB.
5 million, where MPB intersects MSC.
7 million, where MSB meets the vertical axis.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: Society should provide consultations up to the point where the benefit to society equals the cost to society. Compared with the socially optimal quantity, the free market:
answers: Over-provides by 1 million consultations, delivering 6 million rather than 5 million.
Under-provides by 1 million consultations, delivering 5 million rather than 6 million.
Delivers exactly the socially optimal quantity of 5 million consultations.
Under-provides by 2 million consultations, delivering 5 million rather than 7 million.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: Left to market forces alone, only 5 million consultations are provided, instead of the socially optimal 6 million. At that market quantity MSB is $70 while MSC is only $50. What deadweight loss does the unregulated market create?
answers: $20 million, calculated as 1 million × $20.
$100 million, calculated as 5 million × $20.
$5 million, calculated as ½ × 1 million × $10.
$10 million, calculated as ½ × 1 million × $20.

title: Market for GP consultations
questionText: Because this is a positive externality of consumption, the government pays patients a per-unit subsidy for each consultation, raising their demand towards MSB and moving the market to the socially optimal 6 million consultations. How large must the subsidy be, and what will patients pay after receiving it?
answers: A subsidy of $20 per consultation, with patients paying $60 and doctors receiving $40.
A subsidy of $10 per consultation, with patients paying $50 and doctors receiving $60.
A subsidy of $20 per consultation, with patients paying $40 (after the subsidy) and doctors receiving $60.
A subsidy of $60 per consultation, with patients paying nothing.
